Compliance with Mental Capacity Act training was 68.2%. Staff assessed and recorded people’s capacity to consent appropriately. They did this on a decision specific basis about significant decisions.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Delivering evidence-based care and treatment

evidenceCategory.commentary:
Staff planned and delivered people’s care and treatment with them, including what was important and mattered to them. They did this in line with legislation and current evidence based good practice and standards.

Staff provided a comprehensive range of care and treatment interventions tailored to the client group, in line with National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidance. Care was planned and delivered collaboratively with clients, ensuring their preferences and what mattered to them were central to treatment. Systems were in place to keep staff updated with current evidence-based practice and relevant legislation, including the Mental Health Act 1983 and its Code of Practice, which staff understood and applied effectively in their roles. Clinical records demonstrated that care was consistently delivered in accordance with current guidance and best practice standards.


Clients had access to a range of psychological interventions and support, alongside care that promoted emotional wellbeing. Staff also supported clients to maintain good physical health and live healthier lives by encouraging engagement in meaningful activities to develop everyday living skills, as well as access to community resources such as local leisure facilities.


The service used recognised outcome measures, including the Health of the Nation Outcome Scales (HoNOS), to assess and monitor client progress. These were supported by active participation in clinical audit, benchmarking, and quality improvement initiatives. The multidisciplinary team included a full range of specialists required to meet client needs, including doctors, nurses, occupational therapists, clinical psychologists, social workers, pharmacists, dietitians, and support workers. Most staff were appropriately qualified, experienced, and equipped with the skills and knowledge necessary to deliver safe, effective, and holistic care.


Managers in the service supported staff development through structured inductions, including for students, and ensured access to specialist training relevant to their roles. Training compliance for mandatory learning, such as Tier 1, Oliver McGowan training, was high, although completion of some face-to-face training remained in progress. Managers identified staff learning needs and provided opportunities for ongoing development, including planned teaching sessions on clinical topics such as seizures. Regular team meetings were held, where staff discussed ward activities, incidents, complaints, compliments, and learning, with evidence of this reflected in meeting records, supporting a culture of shared learning and continuous improvement.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: How staff, teams and services work together

evidenceCategory.commentary:
Staff held regular and effective multidisciplinary team (MDT) meetings, where information about clients was shared appropriately within the team. We observed a multidisciplinary handover meeting and saw detailed, client focused discussions, with staff sharing updates on clients’ presentation, risks, and required levels of support.


Staff discussed any new and emerging risks, as well as ongoing care needs, and ensured that all relevant information was communicated clearly to those attending. This included updates on client activities, involvement from external professionals, and plans for ongoing care and support.


There were effective handover processes, including shift to shift handovers, which supported continuity of care and ensured staff had up to date information clients.


The service demonstrated positive multidisciplinary working, with effective communication and collaboration both within the team and with external organisations. Staff had good working relationships with partner agencies, including GP services, community mental health teams, pharmacies, and local authority services. This supported safe care delivery, coordinated care planning, and smooth transitions between services.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Monitoring and improving outcomes

evidenceCategory.commentary:
Staff routinely monitored people’s care and treatment to continuously improve it. They ensured that outcomes were positive and consistent, and that they met both clinical expectations and the expectations of people themselves.


Staff routinely monitored people’s care and treatment to drive continuous improvement, ensuring outcomes were positive, consistent, and aligned with both clinical expectations and the needs and preferences of clients within the service.

Care delivery was responsive to client acuity, supported by flexible staffing arrangements and structured ward routines. Family involvement was actively encouraged through structured forums and regular communication opportunities, promoting inclusive care planning. We reviewed five care and treatment records and found staff used recognised rating scales where indicated, such as AUDIT-C, SADQ and COWS, to support assessment and monitoring.

A robust audit framework was in place to review and improve practice. Care planning and risk assessment audits examined the quality, completeness, and individualisation of records. Audits of restrictive practices ensured any restrictions were proportionate, justified, and evidence based, while physical health audits monitored the identification, escalation, and integration of physical healthcare needs within care pathways. Observation and engagement audits assessed whether clients were appropriately observed and meaningfully engaged in therapeutic activity to support recovery.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Supporting people to live healthier lives

evidenceCategory.commentary:
Staff supported people to manage their health and wellbeing to fully maximise their independence, choice and control. Staff supported people to live healthier lives and where possible, reduce their future needs for care and support.


Ward activities supported clients to live healthier lifestyles. These included walking groups, yoga and other physical activities, alongside structured therapeutic interventions such as relapse prevention, recovery planning, 12-step meetings, mindfulness, and emotional regulation work through Dialectical Behaviour Therapy (DBT).

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

keyQuestionRatings.name: Responsive
keyQuestionRatings.commentary:
We looked for evidence that the service met people’s needs, and that staff treated people equally and without discrimination.


At our last assessment we rated this key question good. At this inspection, the rating has remained the same.


Clients did not have to stay in hospital when they completed the treatment programme. The design, layout, and furnishings of the ward supported clients’ treatment, privacy and dignity. Staff supported clients with activities outside the service, such as work, education and family relationships. The service met the needs of all clients including those with a protected characteristic. Staff helped clients with communication, advocacy and cultural and spiritual support. The service treated concerns and complaints seriously, investigated them and learned lessons from the results.

topicareas.name: Care provision, Integration and continuity

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service understood the diverse health and care needs of people and their local communities, so care was joined up, flexible and supported choice and continuity.


Staff ensured that clients who were able, could access activities in the community. For example, day trips, and visits to community places.


Staff supported clients to maintain contact with their families and carers. Carers told us they were in regular contact with their loved ones and could visit regularly.


The service encouraged cultural differences through, religious cultural practices, and diversity focus groups.
Staff said they had good working relationships with external professionals. Care records demonstrated that staff routinely recorded updates and feedback from external professionals and services involved in people’s care. This ensured relevant information was shared, actions were followed up on, and care remained coordinated and responsive to people’s changing needs.


On discharge from the service the provider, provided one full year of aftercare, which typically included group-based peer support.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Equity in access

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service actively sought out and listened to information about people who were most likely to experience inequality in experience or outcomes. They tailored the care, support and treatment in response to this.


Overall, the service had a 100% completion rate of training in equality, diversity, and inclusion.


Staff told us the service was inclusive of people from diverse backgrounds.


The provider had policies in place to ensure people were treated equally. There were opportunities for clients to give feedback about their care and support. There were opportunities for clients to give feedback anonymously via a survey.


Wheelchair accessible rooms were provided for individuals with mobility difficulties.


There was adequate medical cover day and night. A doctor could attend the ward quickly in an emergency.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Equity in experiences and outcomes

evidenceCategory.commentary:
Staff and leaders actively listened to information about people who are most likely to experience inequality in experience or outcomes and tailored their care, support and treatment in response to this. Staff identified that some people from minority ethnic backgrounds could not complete their medical assessments due to language barriers. In response, interpreters were made available, to improve understanding and trust.


Feedback provided by people using the service, both to the provider as well as to CQC, was positive. Clients told us they felt they were treated fairly and with respect. Staff treated people equally and without discrimination. Staff understood the importance of providing an inclusive approach to care and adjusted support equity in people’s experience and outcomes. Staff received training in equality, diversity, inclusion and human rights.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Listening to and involving people

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service made it easy for people to share feedback and ideas, or raise complaints about their care, treatment and support. Staff involved people in decisions about their care and told them what had changed as a result.


Staff understood the complaints process and were confident in managing concerns appropriately. Managers investigated complaints thoroughly, ensured lessons were learned, and shared outcomes with staff to support improvements in practice.


Staff actively encouraged clients to provide feedback through a range of mechanisms, including community meetings, surveys, and online digital healthcare review platforms. We reviewed community meeting minutes, which showed that client feedback was regularly discussed and escalated to clinical governance meetings. The service had also undertaken client satisfaction surveys, and we saw evidence that results were reviewed and used to inform service improvements. For example, feedback regarding the quality of food had led the service to take appropriate action. During the inspection, we found that the catering provider, Sodexo, was responsive to feedback and took steps to address concerns raised by people using the service.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Person-centred Care

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service made sure people were at the centre of their care and treatment choices and they decided, in partnership with people, how to respond to any relevant changes in people’s needs. Client records showed that staff directed clients to other services where appropriate and, if required, supported them to access those services. This was reflected in feedback from clients, who described being supported with discharge planning and preparation for life after treatment. Clients told us staff discussed aftercare options and referrals as part of their ongoing care, including support with external services and community provision.


One client reported that staff had spoken with them about aftercare and “real life” preparation, while another highlighted support from a therapist in liaising with external agencies and advocating on their behalf. This demonstrated a proactive approach to coordinating care and supporting clients to access wider services beyond the immediate setting.


The service supported people to achieve abstinence from drugs and alcohol, Staff we spoke with shared examples of how they based care and treatment around individual needs and preferences. Staff told us how they used a person-centred approach, asking clients what they would find helpful and agreeing achievable and holistic goals with them.


Each client has their own bedroom, equipped with an ensuite bathroom and privacy windows they could adjust.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Planning for the future

evidenceCategory.commentary:
Our records review showed people were supported to consider their wishes for their future. This included discussions about long term recovery goals, and family relationships. Staff recorded these preferences in care plans and shared relevant information with other services when necessary to ensure continuity of care and respect for individual choices.


Staff told us they encouraged people to think about what mattered most to them beyond treatment, such as aspirations for education, work, and rebuilding social networks. Where appropriate, these plans were linked to community resources.


We saw examples where future planning was integrated into multidisciplinary team discussions, ensuring that professionals across health, and social care, contributed to coordinated support. This approach helped people transition smoothly between services and reduced the risk of disengagement.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Providing Information

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service provided appropriate, accurate and up to date information in formats that were tailored to individual needs. The information provided was in a form accessible to client group.


Information was provided in easy read formats.


Staff ensured that clients could obtain information on treatments, local services, clients’ rights, and how to complain.


Staff made notifications to external bodies as needed, we saw the service recorded their referrals and outcomes.


Information governance systems included confidentiality of client records.


We observed posters in relation to clients’ rights and how to complain. Staff completed a daily information board for clients. This included how many staff were working each day.


Staff made appropriate notifications to external bodies.

Staff ensured carers and families and were regularly updated about the patient’s progress with individual consent.


The service provides weekly support group to keep carers and families informed.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

keyQuestionRatings.name: Safe
keyQuestionRatings.commentary:
This means we looked for evidence that people were protected from abuse and avoidable harm.


At our last assessment in June 2021, we rated this key question as Good. At this assessment, the key question has been rated as requires improvement.


The service was in breach of Regulation 12: Safe Care and Treatment and Regulation 18: Staffing.


Some aspects of the service were not always safe. The provider did not ensure that staff had the necessary training and competence to safely deliver substance misuse care, including the management of withdrawal and opioid overdose. This impacted on staff’s ability to recognise and respond to deteriorating clients and to administer emergency treatment, such as naloxone, in a timely way.


Although systems for the management of medicines were in place, staff knowledge and access to emergency medicines were not always sufficient to ensure safe and effective care.


The service had access to a range of professionals to meet people’s needs; however, this did not mitigate the risks arising from gaps in staff competence and the deployment of staff without the required training.
keyQuestionRatings.narrative: This service is not always safe

topicareas.name: Infection prevention and control

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service assessed and managed the risk of infection. They prevented and controlled the risk of it spreading and shared concerns with appropriate agencies promptly.


Staff maintained equipment well and kept it clean. We observed all ward areas were clean, tidy and kept well maintained.


The service carries out regular Infection, Prevention and Control audits. These included cleanliness for all areas both client and non-client areas, hand hygiene, mattress audit and an annual compliance audit. At the time of our assessment, Infection Prevention Control compliance rate was 87.5%.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Involving people to manage risks

evidenceCategory.commentary:
Staff worked with people to understand and manage risks by thinking holistically. Staff provided care to meet people’s needs that was safe, supportive and enabled people to do the things that mattered to them.


During the assessment, we reviewed 5 risk assessments and saw that clients had a risk assessment in place on admission, and these were thorough and regularly updated. There were management plans in place for identified risks and needs of individuals. However, 5 out of 5 did not have a contingency plan for any unexpected exits.


Staff provided care to meet people’s needs in a safe and supportive manner and enabled people to do the things that mattered to them. There was evidence of appropriate restrictions to manage individual risks that had been care planned.


Staff could clearly explain the procedures for supportive observations and engagement.


Staff understood their responsibilities to manage emergencies and to recognise those in need of urgent medical attention.


Staff discussed risks to clients in a range of forums. In the meetings we observed, staff shared updates about risks to and from clients.

Staff communicated with clients clearly so that they understood their care and treatment. Staff had easy access to an interpreter service.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Learning culture

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider had established policies and procedures for staff to report incidents, near misses, and safety events. Staff we spoke with knew what incidents to report and how to report them. Examples included escalation of relapses via Datix and safeguarding concerns being raised promptly. Some safeguarding examples involved parental substance misuse and assessment of immediate risk within family environments.


The service had established several systems to share learning and best practice, this included daily and monthly meetings, with handovers occurring regularly. Some staff mentioned joint sessions with the ward team to share risks and changes in presentation.


We attended handover on Lower court ward and saw that individual risks and incidents were shared with staff.


Staff reported that they were debriefed and received appropriate support following incidents. However, less experienced staff described limited involvement in incident reporting processes and had not yet received feedback from investigations. In contrast, more experienced staff were able to evidence engagement with lessons learned and reported receiving regular updates through clinical governance processes.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Medicines optimisation

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service made sure that medicines and treatments were safe and met people’s needs, capacities and preferences by enabling them to be involved in planning, including when changes happened.


The service had systems and processes in place to safely administer, and record medicines use. Staff followed clear systems for prescribing, storing and administering medicines. Medicines including controlled drugs were stored safely and securely. Staff had access to emergency medicines if needed.


Care and treatment were person‑centred. Prescribing and detox regimens were individualised and followed recognised national protocols. People were involved in decisions about their treatment, and their preferences were considered as part of care planning. Staff used both medical and therapeutic approaches to support recovery. Doses were titrated in response to clinical need. Staff monitored for side effects and recorded these in the care record. PRN (when required) medicines were used appropriately. The care records showed reasons for use, associated risk assessments and relevant physical health checks. Most PRN use was for short‑term symptom relief such as sleep or anxiety and was reviewed. At the time of our assessment, Safe Handling of Medicines compliance rate was 100%.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Safe and effective staffing

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not ensure that sufficient numbers of staff with the appropriate qualifications, competence, skills and experience were available to safely meet the needs of people using the service. At the time of inspection, only 52% of staff had completed mandatory medically assisted withdrawal (MAW) training. Staff we spoke to demonstrated gaps in key substance misuse competencies, including recognising the signs and symptoms of withdrawal. Staff we spoke with were unable to describe opioid withdrawal symptoms, and none had received training in the use of naloxone. Naloxone is a life‑saving medicine used to rapidly reverse the effects of an opioid overdose. A review of the duty rota identified three shifts where all staff on duty lacked mandatory substance misuse training, indicating that staff without the required competence were routinely deployed. These gaps in training and competence posed a potential risk to client safety. Staff we spoke with were unable to identify the signs of opioid overdose, were unclear how to administer naloxone and could not confirm its location within the clinical area. Although staff told us that a doctor was available 24 hours a day to administer naloxone if required, this reliance on medical staff did not mitigate the risks associated with the lack of knowledge, competence and immediate response capability among ward-based staff. If the doctor was attending an emergency elsewhere, this created a risk of delay in administering life-saving treatment.


Some staff did not consistently recognise or respond appropriately to clinical risk and physical health deterioration, including withdrawal symptoms. We found that initial assessment processes did not always identify or address substance related risks. For example, 1 client was admitted at 4pm and although an assessment was completed by staff on admission this did not comprehensively address the client’s current needs and risks. A documented formulation and management plan was not developed in response to the client’s identified risks of alcohol use and withdrawals. A withdrawal screening tool was not completed on admission, and an assisted withdrawal plan was not developed. A doctor was contacted three hours after the client’s admission due to them experiencing physical deterioration and symptoms of withdrawal, requiring urgent medication and development of a medication detox regimen. We discussed this case with staff, and it was noted that there had been a delay in sufficient monitoring and a lack of timely response to escalating risks.


Following the inspection, the provider reported that compliance with medically assisted withdrawal (MAW) training had been achieved. The provider also confirmed that their medicines policy had been updated and re-approved to include the location of naloxone, and that nursing staff could administer it without a prescription, and nursing staff had now been trained to administer naloxone.


Staff had received and were up to date with all other mandatory training courses. The training was appropriate for the patient group using the service, with an overall compliance rate of 83.6% at the time of the assessment, and systems in place to monitor training due to expire. High compliance of 100% was seen in safeguarding adults and children, complaints management, diversity and inclusion, medicines management, health and safety and basic life support.


Supervision compliance was variable, with strong performance mid-year but a notable decline towards end of 2025, particularly for managerial supervision. In December, clinical supervision compliance was 60% and managerial supervision 18.75%. Newer staff stated that supervision was still in the early stages and they were unsure of its benefit. These factors contributed to inconsistency in practice and a lack of confidence across the team. Despite this, systems were in place to provide both clinical and managerial supervision, and records showed that staff were receiving supervision, although not always in line with expected timeframes.


Safe recruitment processes were in place, with appropriate Disclosure and Barring Service (DBS) checks undertaken. The multidisciplinary team was well resourced and included doctors, nurses, occupational therapists, clinical psychologists, providing a range of specialist roles that met the needs of the client group. There was medical cover at all times, with a doctor able to attend quickly in an emergency and a visible clinical presence during the inspection.


Staff participated in appraisal processes. Staffing levels enabled clients to access regular one to one time, and there were enough staff to complete required physical interventions such as observations. The service also demonstrated strong workforce stability. Staff turnover throughout 2025 remained low, generally between 0-2% per month, with minimal unplanned movement. Four staff left in January 2026 due to planned redundancies, indicating managed organisational change rather than instability. The service had significantly reduced its reliance on agency staff, with usage steadily decreasing from July 2025 and reaching zero in November and December 2025. Bank staff were used appropriately to maintain safe staffing levels, supporting continuity of care and reducing risks associated with unfamiliar staff.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Safe environments

evidenceCategory.commentary:
Fire Risk assessments were in place, and fire drills did occur. Staff involved the necessary healthcare and social care services to support clients, where necessary.


The ward environment was clean, tidy, well-furnished and well maintained. Staff carried out daily environmental checks to identify risks and ensure timely repairs.


The ward layout supported effective observation of clients. While some areas were not directly visible from the nursing station, staff mitigated risks through the use of CCTV and mirrors. CCTV signage was clearly displayed throughout the service.


Staff completed regular environmental and ligature risk assessments, which were up to date and covered both internal and external areas. Staff demonstrated awareness of ligature anchor points and understood how to manage and mitigate these risks. Individual risk assessments were used effectively to identify and reduce risks to clients based on their needs. Staff completed daily and weekly ward checks of the environmental and equipment. Client observation records were fully completed with no gaps identified. Staff had a clear understanding of the different levels of engagement and observations to manage client risk.


Staff had access to alarms, and clients could easily access nurse call systems, supporting timely response to risk.
The service complied with same sex accommodation guidance, with all clients accommodated in single occupancy bedrooms with en-suite facilities.


Fire safety arrangements were robust, with up-to-date fire risk assessments, regular fire drills, and weekly fire alarm testing in place.


Clients had access to a range of communal and therapeutic spaces, including lounges, quiet areas, a female only area, and designated therapy and activity rooms. There was also access to a well-maintained outdoor space with seating and recreational facilities.


Clinic rooms were fully equipped, with accessible resuscitation equipment and emergency medicines, which were regularly checked by staff.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Safe systems, pathways and transitions

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service worked with people and their partners to establish and maintain safe systems continuity of care, including when people moved between different services.


The service did not have clearly defined admission criteria within the policies reviewed. Although referrals were discussed within the clinical and therapy teams, this did not mitigate the absence of clear, documented criteria. This lack of structure increased the risk of inconsistent decision making and increased the potential for clients to be admitted without a clearly documented or robust clinical rationale.


Across the records, there was evidence of good physical health assessment and regular use of clinical monitoring tools such as CIWA and NEWS2. Care plans in several cases were responsive and updated regularly, and consent to share information was documented. Multidisciplinary team (MDT) meetings included a range of professionals who contributed to discussions and decision making. Appropriate safety policies were in place, including safeguarding and infection prevention and control policies. Some records showed effective involvement of MDTs and partner or family participation, and examples of extended post discharge support were evident. Monitoring for alcohol and opiate withdrawal was recorded in clients’ records, and clients with more complex needs, such as HIV management, had relevant treatment pathways recorded within their notes.


The service had operational procedures in place to support safe systems, transitions and pathways for treatment and recovery. Staff worked within multidisciplinary teams including, nursing staff, occupational therapists, and psychologists, they worked well together to look at the client pathway and delivery of care.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Safeguarding

evidenceCategory.commentary:
Overall staff worked with people and healthcare partners to understand what being safe meant to them and the best way to achieve that. Staff concentrated on improving people’s lives while protecting their right to live in safety, free from bullying, harassment, abuse, discrimination, avoidable harm and neglect.


The service’s processes promoted people living free from abuse, neglect, and avoidable harm. We saw clear evidence that systems, policies, and practices were in place to safeguard people effectively. The service had a comprehensive safeguarding procedure and a range of supporting policies covering both adults and children.


Staff received safeguarding training and understood how to raise a safeguarding alert. They were aware of the safeguarding leads within the service. However, not all staff were consistently able to clearly articulate safeguarding concerns or provide client specific examples relevant to the ward. Leaders recognised this and had taken action to strengthen safeguarding practice. This included introducing monthly safeguarding workshops supported by senior clinical leads, implementing competency assessments for relevant staff, and embedding safeguarding into monthly quality walkarounds to test knowledge and support ongoing oversight.


Staff were up to date with mandatory safeguarding training for both adults and children, with training compliance at 100% at the time of the assessment. Staff were also either up to date with, actively undertaking, or had been allocated the training for completion in the Mental Capacity Act, Mental Health Act, and the Oliver McGowan Mandatory Training on Learning Disability and Autism, supporting their ability to provide safe and person-centred care.


We reviewed the service safeguarding log covering January 2025 to December 2025. During this period, four safeguarding concerns were formally reported. Each record clearly outlined the concern raised, immediate action taken, and the outcome. We saw evidence of effective collaborative working with partner agencies to ensure people were safeguarded appropriately.


Safeguarding information and advocacy details were accessible, up to date, and clearly displayed for clients and carers. This supported people to be informed, involved, and protected.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

keyQuestionRatings.name: Well-led
keyQuestionRatings.commentary:
We looked for evidence that service leadership, management and governance assured high-quality, person-centred care; supported learning and innovation; and promoted an open and inclusive culture.


This key question has been rated as good.


The service was in breach of Regulation 17: Good Governance.


Leaders were visible and approachable, and some staff described a culture where they felt able to speak up. However, governance systems did not always operate effectively to ensure the quality and safety of care. Although systems for oversight and assurance were in place, they had not consistently identified or addressed risks relating to staff competence, training and the safe delivery of substance misuse care in a timely way.


As a result, some risks to people using the service, including gaps in staff knowledge and the management of clinical deterioration and overdose, were not consistently identified or addressed prior to the inspection.


Leaders demonstrated awareness of areas for improvement and acted on feedback during the inspection. Following the inspection, they took action to strengthen staff knowledge and competence in key areas of substance misuse care. However, opportunities had been missed to identify and address some concerns through existing governance and assurance processes before the inspection.

topicareas.name: Capable, compassionate and inclusive leaders

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service had an inclusive leader who understood the context in which they delivered care, treatment and support and embodied the culture and values of their workforce and organisation.


Leaders did not consistently demonstrate effective oversight of staffing, skill mix, and clinical risk within the service. This indicated that leaders’ knowledge of substance misuse practice and associated clinical risks was limited. While some leaders were open and transparent during the inspection, there were gaps in their awareness and proactive management of key risks. For example, senior leaders acknowledged that they had not fully considered mitigations for skill mix concerns until these were highlighted during the inspection, despite ongoing issues related to staff sickness, lateness, and staffing pressures.


Staff feedback indicated inconsistent experiences of leadership support. Interviews with staff, highlighted ongoing concerns about staffing levels and skill mix, with some staff reporting that the ward did not feel safely staffed at least twice per week. We followed this up with leaders, who acknowledged the concerns and outlined plans to address them through training and improving skill mix. However, staff feedback indicated these measures had not yet ensured consistent staffing levels. They also described instances where a preceptorship nurse was required to take charge of the shift.


There were also concerns regarding the availability of senior clinical leadership. Staff reported occasions where no senior clinical leadership cover was available when senior staff were off shift, which reduced opportunities for escalation, support, and clinical decision making.


Following the inspection, the provider took action to address identified gaps by implementing additional training for qualified nursing staff to ensure they are competent in recognising and responding to opioid overdose, including the safe and effective use of naloxone in emergency situations.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Freedom to speak up

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service promoted an open and positive culture. Staff and people told us they felt able to speak up and believed their views would be listened to and acted upon. This was supported by feedback during the inspection, where staff described feeling safe to raise issues without fear of reprisal.


The provider had policies and processes in place to support freedom to speak up, and staff were aware of these. We saw evidence that learning from incidents and complaints was shared in team meetings, and staff were encouraged to contribute to discussions about service improvements.


This approach demonstrated some openness to feedback and an intention to improve; however, it was not consistently embedded, and concerns were not always addressed promptly or effectively.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Governance, management and sustainability

evidenceCategory.commentary:
Governance systems were not fully effective in identifying, monitoring and addressing risks relating to staff competence, training and the safe delivery of care. Although governance processes were in place, these had not consistently ensured that all staff had the knowledge, skills and training required to safely deliver substance misuse treatment, including the management of withdrawal and opioid overdose.


Oversight of workforce competence and deployment was not always sufficient. Governance processes had not identified or addressed low compliance with mandatory medically assisted withdrawal (MAW) training, the deployment of staff without the appropriate competence, or gaps in staff knowledge relating to the use of naloxone and access to naloxone. Leaders acknowledged that mitigations for skill mix concerns had not been fully considered prior to the inspection.


While leaders had implemented training programmes, including the Oliver McGowan training, there were gaps in ensuring staff competence in critical clinical areas. Staff across roles, including registered nurses and healthcare assistants, were unable to identify the signs of opioid overdose or describe the use of naloxone, which is essential knowledge within this service context. This demonstrated that training arrangements had not consistently ensured staff competence in all key areas of practice.


Audit findings were translated into local and divisional action plans, showing that governance structures were in place to support learning and service improvement. Staff were able to demonstrate how audit outcomes informed planned actions. However, systems for monitoring the quality and safety of care had not identified or addressed all of the concerns highlighted during the inspection, including staffing gaps, knowledge deficits and inconsistencies in care delivery. This reduced the provider's ability to identify and respond to risks in a timely way. While governance arrangements supported some oversight and improvement activity, they were not consistently effective in assuring safety, quality and continuous improvement.


Leaders acknowledged areas requiring improvement and responded to feedback during the inspection. Following the inspection, the provider reported taking action to address identified gaps, including implementing targeted training for nursing staff to improve competence in recognising and responding to opioid overdose and the wider administration of naloxone in emergency situations, alongside wider actions to strengthen staff knowledge in substance misuse and withdrawal management.


Although these actions demonstrated a willingness to learn and improve, they were implemented following concerns identified during the inspection. This showed that existing governance and assurance processes had not consistently identified and addressed these issues at an earlier stage.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Learning, improvement and innovation

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The evidence showed some shortfalls. The service did not consistently demonstrate effective systems to support continuous learning, improvement and innovation across the organisation. Processes were not always effective in identifying and responding to risks in a timely way, which limited opportunities to drive improvement in the quality and safety of care.


The service had some processes to support learning and improvement, but these were not consistently effective in identifying and addressing risks in a timely way.


Staff told us they were able to contribute ideas for improvement through team meetings, and opportunities for professional development, including specialist training and apprenticeships, were available. However, there was limited evidence that learning from incidents, audits or feedback was embedded into routine practice or used to deliver sustained, measurable improvements.

Although some monitoring and assurance systems were in place, they had not driven timely improvements in areas of concern. This limited the service’s ability to use learning to proactively improve the quality and safety of care.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Partnerships and communities

evidenceCategory.commentary: The service demonstrated a clear understanding of its responsibility to collaborate and work in partnership. Information and learning were consistently shared with a range of partners including hospitals services, GPs, local authorities, and mental health services. The provider shared examples of community engagement and harm reduction initiatives. Such as signposting or referring clients to community recovery groups and peer support networks (e.g. 12-step programmes).

asgRatings.name: Residential substance misuse services
asgRatings.commentary:
The Priory Hospital Hayes Grove is an independent hospital providing inpatient care and treatment for adults with mental health conditions, eating disorders and substance misuse needs. The service provides care for men and women aged 18 and over, with a total of 46 inpatient beds.

Lower Court is an acute private inpatient client ward providing care for up to 17 men and women. The ward supports individuals requiring treatment for mental health conditions as well as those engaging in the specialist addictions programme. 

Clients on Lower Court ward are encouraged to take increasing responsibility for their recovery as they progress through their admission, with a particular focus on structured discharge planning. A range of individual and group therapeutic interventions is available throughout their stay.

The ward environment is designed to be safe, therapeutic and recovery-oriented, while maintaining dignity, privacy and inclusivity across genders.

The ward’s philosophy centres on compassionate; recovery focused, evidence-based care delivered within a structured and supportive setting. Its therapeutic model integrates medical oversight with psychological therapies, emphasising patient-centred practice. The service aims to build resilience, promote independence, and equip individuals with the skills required to maintain recovery and successfully reintegrate clients into the community.

The service is registered to provide care for the following regulated activities:

Accommodation for persons who require treatment for substance misuse

• Assessment or medical treatment for persons detained under the Mental Health Act 1983

• Diagnostic and screening procedures

• Treatment of disease, disorder or injury

The service had a registered manager in place at the time of this inspection. 

This was an announced focused inspection of the service. We looked at two domains safe and well led.

At the time of the assessment, 9 people were receiving treatment for substance misuse at the service.

We spoke with 6 staff members, 3 patients. We also reviewed the care and treatment records of 4 patients.

At our previous assessment, the overall location rating is Good. The key question Safe was Requires Improvement, the key questions Effective, Caring and Responsive and Well-Led was Good. 

At this assessment, the overall location rating is Good. The key question Safe has changed to Good. The key questions Effective, Caring, Responsive and Well-Led have remained Good. 

The team that inspected the service comprised of 2 CQC Inspectors. 

We found the following areas of good practice:

  • The service developed holistic, recovery-oriented care plans informed by a comprehensive assessment.
  • The service had ensured that staff had received the necessary training appropriate to the client group.
  • We saw evidence of client centred discussions in Multi-Disciplinary Team (MDT) meetings.
  • People and carers praised the staff as incredibly professional, sharing their view that The Priory Hospital Hayes Grove “helpful, and supportive.”

 

Mental Capacity Act Compliance

Mental Capacity Act

The service delivered care within a clear legal framework with appropriate application of the Mental Capacity Act and robust consent processes supporting safe and effective care for informal clients.

Staff completed capacity assessments on admission and demonstrated an understanding of the Mental Capacity Act 2005, and its five statutory principles. Staff demonstrated an understanding of the impact on capacity when under the influence of substances, and how this was managed. 

Clients were provided with clear explanations about their care and treatment and given sufficient time to consider information before consenting.

Staff applied the principles of the Mental Capacity Act 2005 in practice. Staff followed service policy when assessing and recording capacity, and documentation demonstrated that clients were supported to make informed decisions.

The service delivered care within an appropriate legal framework for informal clients.

Training in both the Mental Capacity Act and Mental Health Act was mandatory. Compliance with Mental Capacity Act training was 72.7% at the time of inspection, while Mental Health Act training compliance was 70%. Remaining staff were booked on for training soon after the inspection. The service also informed us that training had been planned to support ongoing improvements and development of staff practice. Improvements were required to ensure full compliance with mandatory training, particularly in relation to the Mental Health Act, to support consistent and up-to-date documentation.

Overall, people spoke very positively about the service, consistently describing staff as helpful and supportive. All clients reported that they felt safe, well informed about their care and treatment, and treated as individuals. Care and treatment were frequently described as life changing, with some clients stating it had “saved their life” and exceeded expectations. Clients particularly valued the structured therapeutic programmes and the supportive relationships formed with staff.

topicareas.name: Safe and effective staffing

evidenceCategory.commentary:
Since our last inspection the provider had made changes to address areas of concern identified. We saw that the provider now ensured that sufficient numbers of staff with the appropriate qualifications, competence, skills and experience were available to safely meet the needs of people using the service.

The last time we inspected, only 52% of staff had completed mandatory medically assisted withdrawal (MAW) training. At this inspection 92% of staff had completed this training. At our last inspection, staff we spoke with demonstrated gaps in key substance misuse competencies, including recognising the signs and symptoms of withdrawal. At this inspection all staff we spoke with were able to describe opioid withdrawal symptoms and had received training in the use of naloxone. Naloxone is a life‑saving medicine used to rapidly reverse the effects of an opioid overdose. Staff we spoke with were able to identify the signs of opioid overdose, were clear how to administer naloxone and could confirm its location within the clinical area. The service had introduced a section in daily team meetings where staff were asked to describe signs of withdrawal, in order to assess their knowledge. There was an information poster on the wall in the clinic room outlining withdrawal symptoms.  

During this assessment, information we looked at indicated staff were able to recognise and respond appropriately to clinical deterioration. Leaders also ensured all staff had completed competency assessments in this area. At our last inspection initial assessment processes did not fully identify or address substance related risks. There was no documented alcohol withdrawal screening or breathalyser test on admission, and although a HoNOS assessment was completed, this focused on routine outcome measures rather than immediate clinical risk. During this assessment we saw evidence of withdrawal screening and breathalysing taking place and being recorded in patient notes. We also saw alcohol and/or substance use, and associated risks were assessed and reflected in the client’s keeping safe plan.

Staff had received and were up to date with all other mandatory training courses. The training was appropriate for the patient group using the service, with an overall compliance rate of 92.3% at the time of the assessment, and systems in place to monitor training due to expire.

High compliance of 100% was seen in safeguarding adults and children, complaints management, crisis management, diversity and inclusion, medicines management, and learning disability training. 

Systems were in place to provide both clinical and managerial supervision, and records showed that staff were receiving supervision. All staff we spoke with stated that they had received regular supervision. Staff stated they used supervision to discuss their role and professional development. Observations of physical healthcare practices were also undertaken.

Safe recruitment processes were in place, with appropriate Disclosure and Barring Service (DBS) checks undertaken. 

The multidisciplinary team was well resourced and included doctors, nurses, occupational therapists, clinical psychologists, providing a range of specialist roles that met the needs of the client group. There was medical cover at all times, with a doctor able to attend quickly in an emergency and a visible clinical presence during the inspection.

Staff participated in appraisal processes. 

Staffing levels enabled clients to access regular one to one time, and there were enough staff to complete required physical interventions such as observations. There were 2 registered mental health nurses on shift during the day and 1 at night. There were 2 healthcare assistants on shift during the day and 2 at night. There was a qualified nurse present in communal areas of the ward at all times. The service also demonstrated strong workforce stability. Staff turnover throughout 2025 remained low, generally between 0–2% per month, with minimal unplanned movement. Four staff left in January 2026 due to planned redundancies, indicating managed organisational change rather than instability. The service had significantly reduced its reliance on agency staff, with usage steadily decreasing from July 2025 and reaching zero in November and December 2025. Bank staff were used appropriately to maintain safe staffing levels, supporting continuity of care and reducing risks associated with unfamiliar staff.

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service worked with people and their partners to establish and maintain safe systems and continuity of care, including when people moved between different services.

At our last inspection the service did not have clearly defined admission criteria within the policies reviewed. During our recent inspection leaders were able to explain the admission criteria. Admission criteria included the presence of a substance misuse need, being medically fit for admission, willingness to engage in treatment, motivation to make positive changes and the ability to provide consent.

Referrals were reviewed and discussed by the clinical and therapy teams. Once they had determined the patients’ needs and if these could be safely met by the service, they were then booked in for an assessment with addiction therapist. A comprehensive assessment was undertaken which included looking at a patient’s history, social circumstances and consent. Staff discussed treatment options with patients.  Following this, contact was made with the patient's GP to obtain relevant health records.  

During our assessment we reviewed 4 records, there was evidence of good physical health assessment and regular use of clinical monitoring tools such as CIWA and NEWS2. Care plans in several cases were responsive and updated regularly, and consent to share information was documented. Care plans were comprehensive and covered 4 areas. These were keeping well, keeping healthy, keeping connected and safe. These were personalised, included individual goals, and clearly reflected patients' wishes. Monitoring for alcohol and opiate withdrawal was recorded in clients’ records.

The service had operational procedures in place to support safe systems, transitions and pathways for treatment and recovery. Staff worked within multidisciplinary teams including, nursing staff, occupational therapists and psychologists, who contributed to discussions and decision making. 

Appropriate safety policies were in place, including safeguarding and infection prevention and control policies.

topicareas.name: Governance, management and sustainability

evidenceCategory.commentary:
Governance systems were effective in identifying, monitoring and addressing risks relating to staff competence, training and the safe delivery of care. Governance processes were in place, these had ensured that all staff had the knowledge, skills and training required to safely deliver substance misuse treatment, including the management of withdrawal and opioid overdose.

Since our last inspection oversight of workforce competence was embedded. The service had addressed the previous low compliance with mandatory medically assisted withdrawal (MAW) training. They had ensured that all staff received training and had the appropriate competence. Since our last inspection staff’s knowledge relating to the use and access of naloxone had improved. Leaders had ensured that since our inspection the skill mix of staff was appropriate for the patients on the ward.

Staff across roles, including registered nurses and healthcare assistants, were able to identify the signs of opioid overdose or describe the use of Naloxone, which is essential knowledge within this service context. This indicated that training was effective and that they had ensured staff competence.

There was a clear framework of what must be discussed at a ward, team or directorate level in team meetings to ensure that essential information, such as learning from incidents and complaints, was shared and discussed. 

Audit findings were translated into local and divisional action plans, showing that governance structures were in place to support learning and service improvement. Staff were able to demonstrate how audit outcomes informed planned actions. 

Staff had implemented recommendations from reviews of incidents, complaints and safeguarding alerts at the service level.  

Staff maintained and had access to the risk register at ward or directorate level. Staff at ward level could escalate concerns when required.  

The service had plans for emergencies. For example, adverse weather or a flu outbreak.  

Staff had access to the equipment and information technology needed to do their work. The information technology infrastructure, including the telephone system, worked well and helped to improve the quality of care.  

Information governance systems included confidentiality of patient records. We identified some wording inaccuracies in 1 patient record and highlighted these to senior staff at the time. Senior staff took this on board and outlined how this would be addressed.

We carried out a comprehensive assessment of The Priory Hospital Hayes Grove eating disorder unit on 13th and 14th January 2026.

The unit was for both male and female patients aged 18+ who required inpatient care for specialist services for people with eating disorders.

The Priory hospital Hayes Grove was last inspected by the CQC in April 2021. The service was rated overall good. For the eating disorder services, Priory Hospital Hayes Grove was rated requires improvement for Safe and there was one breach of regulations in place around the assessment and management of some physical health risks. At this current inspection, we found this has been addressed and Safe is now rated good.

At this assessment we rated the ward as good in all areas of Safe, Effective, Caring, Responsive and Well-Led care.

We spoke with 9 members of staff, 5 patients and 3 carers. We also reviewed the care and treatment records of 6 patients.
asgRatings.narrative: The service is performing well and meeting our expectations.
asgRatings.overallPeopleExperience:
We spoke with 5 patients and 3 carers during this inspection.

The majority of patient feedback was positive. Patients reported that the ward was well-staffed with kind and helpful people. Patients shared that they felt involved in their care and treatment, regularly meeting with their doctor and the multidisciplinary team.

Patients told us about activities they were involved in, including arts and crafts. One patient said that the night staff were not as involved as the day staff in their care but did acknowledge this could have been as most patients are asleep during the night. Most patients said they felt safe on the ward.

We spoke with 3 family members as part of the inspection. All family members were positive about the care and treatment their family member had received as well as themselves. Family members said they could contact the service at any time should they want an update, advice or information.

One family member said the treatment their child received was the best support their child had received from a hospital and even though staff were faced with challenges with managing behaviours, they always showed kindness and compassion.

We observed positive interactions between staff and patients during the inspection. We saw that staff were kind towards patients. Senior staff highlighted a culture of compassion amongst the team and stated that the team felt like a family.

Mental Health Act

The hospital admitted patients under the Mental Health Act 1983. At the time of the inspection, no patients were detained in hospital for an assessment, and three patients were detained for treatment. Five patients were not detained under the Act.

Staff maintained up-to-date training on the Mental Health Act and staff were able to apply the principles of the Mental Health Act effectively. Training on the Mental Health Act was mandatory for staff, and the compliance rate was 92.3%.

Staff ensured that each patient was informed about their rights under the Mental Health Act, and this was observed within the patients notes.

Staff facilitated section 17 leave (permission to leave the hospital) for patients when agreed upon with the responsible clinician. Section 17 leave arrangements were discussed and organised at the daily handover meeting, which we observed whilst on site.

Detention papers and associated records were accurately stored and readily accessible to staff on the ward as needed. For one patient intramuscular rapid tranquilisation was included on the T2 without a clear rationale about how this would be used in practice. There was no care planning to support its use. This was flagged with senior management on day 1 of our inspection and evidence was observed on day 2 of the inspection, that this had since been amended.

Mental Capacity Act

Training on the Mental Capacity Act was mandatory for staff and 92.3% of staff had completed this.

Staff completed an assessment of each patient’s capacity to consent to admission and treatment on admission. Staff supported patients in making informed decisions about their care and treatment. They demonstrated an understanding of the Mental Capacity Act (MCA) 2005, including its five core principles, and followed provider policy for assessing and recording capacity. Records evidenced that patients got thorough explanations and adequate time to process information before consenting to treatment.

Most patients were positive when talking about the staff and the care they had received from staff and the service. Patients told us they felt listened to and that staff were patient and supportive. Carers told us that they had supported their loved ones in treatment before, but they had not felt as positive about the future until they came to Hayes Grove. topicareas.name: Responding to people’s immediate needs

evidenceCategory.commentary:

Patients shared that they felt the food provided did not meet their needs and reported there was issues with requested meals and food options at times, patients shared that food would be provided that was not on their specific meal plan or food would not look appetising or would be cold.

Staff were aware of the specific risks related to the patient group. For example, significant changes in weight, re-feeding syndrome and the need for physical health monitoring. Staff had received extensive training in working with the patient group. Staff are required to complete 4-day face to face eating disorder course 77.6% of staff have completed this training

Staff were aware of and dealt with any specific risk issues, relating to patients. Staff knew and understood high risk dates and events and could confidently support patients through challenges.

Staff used de-escalation techniques to reduce the need for physical interventions when patients’ behaviour became heightened. Staff engaged patients and used their understanding of the individual and established relationships to manage behaviours before considering any physical intervention.

There had been 23 situations in the last 6 months where staff had used holds to restrain a patient, 18 of these physical restraints were linked to one patient and the need for them to be nasogastric fed.
